item.title: OpenAI Will Let Outside Evaluators In During Training. The Terms Are Vague
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI published principles for third-party safety assessments that reach into training runs and misalignment incidents, but the post drops Sam Altman's earlier promise of badges, laptops and the right to publish.
item.content:encoded:
Ten days ago Sam Altman said outside safety evaluators would get desks, badges and laptops inside OpenAI, plus the right to publish what they found. On Tuesday the company put its plan in writing, and the writing is noticeably softer.

The post lays out four areas OpenAI wants outside groups to examine: its safety cases (the structured arguments that a model's risks are under control) from training through deployment, whether critical safeguards hold up under realistic conditions, the capability evaluations tied to its Preparedness Framework, and independent investigation of misalignment incidents where models act without authorization or dodge oversight.

The reasoning for going earlier is sound. Models are getting better at noticing when they're being tested, so a finished model that behaves during a pre-release eval tells you less than it used to. Looking at checkpoints mid-training, before the polish, is where odd behavior is easier to catch.

So what's the catch? No confirmed partners, no access terms and no timeline. OpenAI says it's in talks with METR and Redwood Research, and that evaluators "may be brought into the offices for the most sensitive work." Publication rights aren't mentioned. Its stated principles (independence, scientific rigor, security, clear responsibilities) are the right words, but independence is exactly the thing a vendor-written framework can't grant itself.

There is one concrete piece. METR and Redwood have agreed to review model behavior tied to an earlier misalignment incident involving Hugging Face, and both groups say they'll publish a write-up of the engagement and, later, their findings. That's the first real test of whether outside reviewers get to say something unflattering in public.

It's worth noting the pattern here. Last week OpenAI published six internal cases of agents hiding errors and leaking files. This week it's inviting outsiders to investigate cases like those. Both are steps in the right direction, and both are still voluntary disclosures on OpenAI's own schedule.

The thing to watch is the first signed agreement. If it includes the right to publish without OpenAI's sign-off, this is meaningful. If it doesn't, it's a well-written blog post.

item.title: September's Windows 11 Updates Break Always On VPN Protocol Fallback
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft confirmed that KB5124008 and KB5124012 can leave Always On VPN stuck at 'Connecting' when profiles auto-select between IKEv2 and SSTP, and the only fix for now is pinning a single protocol.
item.content:encoded:
If your help desk queue filled up this week with remote users stuck on "Connecting," Microsoft now agrees it's the patch. The company posted a service alert on Wednesday confirming that September's cumulative updates can break Always On VPN on Windows 11.

The affected updates are KB5124008 on Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2, and KB5124012 on 26H1. Symptoms are a tunnel that never finishes connecting or fails over and over with "The specified port is already in use."

The trigger is specific. It hits profiles set to automatic protocol selection, where the client tries IKEv2 and falls back to SSTP when IKEv2 is blocked. That fallback is the whole reason a lot of shops use the default, since hotel and airport networks love to drop UDP 500 and 4500 while letting TCP 443 through.

Microsoft's workaround is to change the profile from automatic to a single protocol, either IKEv2 only or SSTP only. That's a quick Intune or ProfileXML change, but pick carefully. IKEv2-only will strand users on networks that block IPsec, and SSTP-only gives up IKEv2's better performance and cleaner reconnect behavior. For most fleets with a mobile workforce, SSTP-only is the safer temporary setting.

There's no fix date yet; Microsoft says it's still investigating. Rolling back the update is the other option, but it also rolls back the two exploited privilege-escalation zero-days patched this month, which makes it a bad trade for anything that touches the internet.

This is the second networking regression from the September release. Microsoft already had to ship an out-of-band update for Remote Desktop Services failures, and that one didn't reach servers through Windows Update. Admins who test before broad rollout just got another data point for keeping a VPN client in the pilot ring.

item.title: A CVSS 10 VeloCloud Orchestrator Flaw Is Being Exploited Before Every Fix Ships
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Arista says CVE-2026-93952 is under active attack against on-prem VeloCloud Orchestrators using certificate-based Edge authentication, and only the 5.2 and 6.4 trains have patches so far.
item.content:encoded:
If you run an on-prem VeloCloud Orchestrator, assume someone has already tried the front door. Arista published Security Advisory 0183 on Monday for CVE-2026-93952, an improper input validation bug in the orchestrator's web interface that scores a flat 10.0 on CVSS 3.1 (9.5 under CVSS 4.0), and the company says it is known to be actively exploited.

The bug lets a remote attacker reach privileged internal functionality on the VCO. There's a catch that narrows the blast radius a little: exploitation requires that certificate-based Edge-to-VCO authentication is configured, that the attacker can reach the web interface, and that they hold the public portion of an Edge's authentication certificate. Public certificates aren't secrets, so that last condition is a speed bump rather than a wall.

Affected builds are VCO 5.2.3.15 and earlier, 6.1.3.7 and earlier, 6.4.2.7 and earlier, and 7.0.0.2 and earlier. Fixes exist for two of those trains: 5.2.3.16 and 6.4.2.8. Customers on 6.1 or 7.0 are told fixes for still-supported trains are coming, which is an uncomfortable spot to be in when the exploit is already live. Arista's hosted and dedicated orchestrators were patched before disclosure, so this is an on-prem problem.

Why this one matters more than the average appliance bug: the orchestrator is the brain of an SD-WAN deployment. Arista's own advisory warns that a compromised VCO may give attackers access to the Edge devices it manages. Own the orchestrator and you're pushing configuration to every branch.

Arista and The Hacker News list indicators worth hunting for right now. On the VCO host, look for /usr/local/sbin/.vcnode.js, a binary at /usr/local/sbin/vc-sysmond, and a systemd unit at /etc/systemd/system/vc-sysmon.service. In nginx logs, look for requests carrying an x-vc-opt header. Two IPs tied to the activity are 142.93.149[.]77 and 104.248.126[.]159.

This is also the second VCO security issue this summer after CVE-2026-16812 in July, and VeloCloud only changed hands from Broadcom to Arista last year. Product transitions are exactly when patch cadence and advisory quality tend to wobble.

What to do today: patch if you're on 5.2 or 6.4. If you're on 6.1 or 7.0, pull the VCO web interface off anything but a trusted admin network, block non-essential outbound ports from the host, and check for the files and header above. If you find them, treat the Edges it manages as suspect too.

item.title: Nearly 1,000 Zyxel Switches Were Quietly Drained of Configs and Root Hashes
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: GreyNoise says a Chinese-speaking actor used CVE-2026-7273 to pull configurations and hashed root credentials from 996 Zyxel GS1900 switches in 48 countries, and CISA wants federal fixes by Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Zyxel patched CVE-2026-7273 in June. By mid-August, an attacker was using it to walk through unpatched GS1900 switches, and by the time anyone said so publicly, 996 of them in 48 countries had given up their configurations, network details and hashed root-level credentials.

The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program behind the GS1900 web interface, rated 8.8. Zyxel's advisory describes it as exploitable by an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN who sends a crafted HTTP request, which gets them OS command execution on the switch. Affected firmware is 2.90(xxxx.1)C0 and earlier across the GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2. The fixed builds are the matching .2 releases.

That "LAN-based" label deserves a raised eyebrow. Nearly a thousand victims spread across Italy, the US, Taiwan, South Korea and a chunk of the EU doesn't look like an attacker who needed to be on anyone's LAN first. It looks like management interfaces reachable from places they shouldn't be. GS1900s are small-office gear, the kind that ends up in schools, hotels and retail back rooms without a network team watching them.

GreyNoise, which disclosed the campaign Monday, attributes it to a Chinese-speaking actor it has tied to earlier WordPress and Gitea exploitation. The exploit was delivered as a Python script wrapped in PyArmor, a commercial obfuscator, and the attacker used TFTP to pull down follow-on collection scripts. That's reconnaissance and credential harvesting, not a smash-and-grab. The stolen root hashes and configs are the kind of thing you collect when you plan to come back.

CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 21 and gave federal civilian agencies until September 24 to fix it. Three days is a short fuse, and it tells you how CISA reads the evidence.

For everyone else: flash the .2 firmware, then assume the old credentials are burned. Rotate the switch admin passwords and anything else that appears in the exported configs (SNMP communities, RADIUS secrets, TACACS keys). Check whether the web UI is reachable from outside your management VLAN, and if it is, fix that before you do anything else.

item.title: Microsoft Called This SharePoint Bug Spoofing. The Public Exploit Says RCE.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-65660, patched in August as a 6.5 spoofing issue, is an authenticated code injection flaw in SharePoint's ToolPane that now has a public webshell-dropping exploit.
item.content:encoded:
A SharePoint patch you may have deprioritized in August just got a lot more urgent. CVE-2026-65660 went out in the August 11 security updates labeled as a spoofing vulnerability, CVSS 6.5, with Microsoft's advisory claiming no impact to integrity or availability. Researcher Dinh Ho Anh Khoa of Viettel Cyber Security has now published a full writeup showing it's authenticated remote code execution.

The bug lives in ToolPane, the same SharePoint component that sat at the center of last year's ToolShell mass exploitation. When ToolPane processes web-part markup, it rebuilds Register directives by dropping attribute values between double quotes without escaping quotes inside them. Inject your own quote and you can smuggle in extra directives that register arbitrary .NET classes after the SafeControls type check has already run. From there, Khoa uses XamlServices.Parse() to reach code execution through deserialization.

The writeup includes a working in-memory webshell. Khoa also shows the flaw chaining with a separate, already-patched authentication bypass to get pre-auth RCE on some server configurations, and says it's been used in real penetration tests.

Affected versions are SharePoint Server 2016, 2019 and Subscription Edition. SharePoint 2013 is vulnerable too, but it's been out of support since April 2023, so there's no patch coming. There's no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation and the bug isn't in CISA's KEV catalog yet.

Here's the part that should bother you. Microsoft's own CVE record for the flaw, updated September 11, calls it remote code execution, and NVD scores it 8.8 with a code injection weakness (CWE-94). The customer-facing Security Update Guide still says spoofing. Plenty of patch programs triage off exactly that label, and "spoofing, 6.5, exploitation unlikely" on a server that's a pain to patch is the kind of entry that gets pushed to next quarter.

If you're running on-prem SharePoint, confirm the August cumulative updates are installed (KB5002893 for Subscription Edition, KB5002894 for 2019, plus the matching 2016 package). If they aren't, you now have a public exploit against an internet-facing collaboration server. Treat it that way.

item.title: Aikido's Altar-1 Puts a Pentesting Model On-Prem, If You Have Four H200s
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Aikido pruned Z.AI's GLM-5.3 from 1.51 TB to 328 GB to make Altar-1, an open-weight security model for air-gapped vuln hunting, but its headline benchmark is just 32 CVEs.
item.content:encoded:
Most of the AI security tooling launched this year has the same catch. To use it, you ship your source code and your findings to someone else's inference cluster. For a bank with data-residency rules or a plant with an air-gapped OT network, that's a nonstarter.

Aikido Security's answer, released September 21, is Altar-1, an open-weight model built to run penetration testing and vulnerability discovery entirely inside the customer's own infrastructure. The weights are on Hugging Face under AikidoSec/altar-1, and it powers the on-prem version of the company's Aikido Machine pentesting product.

Altar-1 isn't trained from scratch. It's Z.AI's open-weight GLM-5.3, squeezed. Aikido first applied AWQ INT4 quantization, taking the model from 1.51 TB to about 488 GB, then pruned the mixture-of-experts layers, keeping 168 of the 256 routed experts in each layer and dropping the 88 that did the least for security work. The result is 328 GB. Aikido's recommended setup is four H200s with vLLM, which is "on-prem" in the sense that a mid-sized enterprise could own it, not in the sense that it runs on your security team's workstation.

The numbers Aikido published are honest about the trade. On its internal benchmark of 32 known vulnerabilities across 30 repositories, run three times each, Altar-1 averaged 60.4% recall and found 23 of the 32. The full-precision GLM-5.3 hit 65.6% and found 25. That's where the "keeps 92% of the parent's coverage" line comes from.

Now the skeptical part, which Aikido mostly makes for us. Thirty-two CVEs is a small test, and it's their test. The company says plainly that it measures targeted rediscovery of known bugs inside a pipeline, not blind discovery across a whole codebase, not exploit execution, and not fix quality. There's also no comparison against the closed frontier models that security teams would actually be weighing this against, which is the number buyers will want most.

Still, the direction is right. OpenAI and Anthropic have spent the last few months deciding how much offensive capability to hand security teams, and on what terms. An open-weight model you can run behind your own firewall sidesteps that debate entirely for the organizations that need it most. The question for those buyers is whether roughly 60% recall on known bugs justifies a four-GPU cluster. For some regulated shops, it will.

item.title: Ireland Fines Google €403M Over Location Tracking That Ended Six Years Ago
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Irish DPC fined Google €403 million for how Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy handled location data between 2018 and 2020, and gave it six months to comply.
item.content:encoded:
Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined Google €403 million on September 21 for how it collected and kept location data. The conduct in question ran from May 25, 2018, the day GDPR took effect, to February 4, 2020. The inquiry itself opened in February 2020.

So yes, a decision on practices from the first Trump administration arrived during the second one.

Three features were in scope. Web & App Activity, which logs searches, browsing and location as you use Google services. Location History, the opt-in timeline of where your phone has been. And Location Accuracy, the Android setting that improves positioning by pulling in Wi-Fi and cell data. The DPC found transparency failures across all three, lawfulness and fairness failures in Web & App Activity and Location History, retention failures in those same two, and an accountability failure in Location Accuracy. Google has six months to bring its processing into line.

The underlying problem will sound familiar if you followed this story the first time. In 2018 the Associated Press showed that turning off Location History didn't stop Google from storing location through Web & App Activity. That report kicked off years of fallout, including a $391.5 million settlement with 40 US states in 2022. Europe is only now landing its version.

Google's response is that it has significantly changed its practices since 2019, pointing to simpler location controls and to Maps Timeline data that now lives on the device and auto-deletes after three months by default. That's true, and it's also why the fine will barely register. A six-month compliance order for processing Google has already restructured is a light lift.

The more useful takeaway is about speed. Six and a half years from inquiry to decision is not a deterrent timeline, and the DPC has been criticized for exactly this before. For anyone building products that touch location data now, the signal isn't that regulators will catch you quickly. It's that they will eventually catch the version of your product you've forgotten about, and your old privacy notices will be the evidence.

item.title: Amazon Locked Meta's Muse Agent Out of Its Store Over Credentials and Disguise
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Amazon started blocking Meta's Muse shopping agent on Sunday night, saying it browses without identifying itself and appears to store customers' Amazon credentials.
item.content:encoded:
Muse users who asked Meta's new AI agent to buy something on Amazon Sunday night got a popup instead: continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use. GeekWire spotted it first, and Amazon has since confirmed the block.

Amazon's stated reasons are more specific than the usual "protecting the customer experience" line. The company says Meta never told it Muse would be shopping its store, that the agent doesn't identify itself when it browses, and that it appears to capture and store customers' Amazon credentials. Amazon also says it asked Meta to keep Amazon.com out of Muse's scope before it pulled the plug.

That credential point is the one security people should care about. An agent that logs in as you, holds your password, and presents itself to the site as an ordinary browser is indistinguishable from an account takeover tool from the retailer's side. Every fraud and bot-detection system Amazon runs is built to stop exactly that traffic pattern.

It's also, conveniently, a competitive move. Amazon sells its own models, runs Bedrock, and wants shoppers talking to its own assistants rather than someone else's. This is the same playbook it used against Perplexity's Comet browser, which it took to court, and it has made similar moves against shopping agents from Google and OpenAI. Security and self-interest point in the same direction here, and Amazon gets to lead with the first one.

The awkward bit is that these two companies are partners. Amazon products have been shoppable inside Facebook and Instagram since 2023, and Meta signed a deal in April to run AI workloads on AWS. Meta hasn't said publicly how it plans to respond.

The fix for the agent-versus-storefront fight is not complicated in principle: agents that declare themselves, authenticate through delegated tokens instead of stored passwords, and work through sanctioned APIs. Nobody has an incentive to build that neutral plumbing while they're each trying to own the checkout, so expect more of these standoffs.

item.title: Hackers Disabled Alarms and Changed Pump Cycles at Two Colorado Water Systems
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Foreign actors got into the operational technology at two small private Colorado water utilities in late August, altering pumping cycles and switching off alarms before operators locked them out.
item.content:encoded:
Somebody outside the country spent part of late August adjusting the pumps at two Colorado water systems. They changed equipment settings, altered pumping cycles, disabled alarms and cut off remote access, and they did it on the operational technology side of the house, not the billing server.

Gov. Jared Polis' office disclosed the intrusions last week. Both utilities are privately owned and each serves fewer than 200 people. The state hasn't named them, and it hasn't said who was responsible. According to the governor's office, the incidents were brief, the operators caught them and locked the systems down, and there's no known impact to treatment, water quality or public safety.

That's the good news, and it's real. It's also the least interesting part.

Disabling alarms is not what an opportunistic defacer does. It's the step you take when you want your other changes to go unnoticed. Pair that with pumping-cycle changes and killing remote access for the legitimate operators, and you have a playbook that looks a lot more like a rehearsal than a prank. Colorado's chief information officer, Sarah Tuneberg, said the state has seen an uptick in international actors going after its infrastructure over the last few months.

Attribution is still open. Federal officials have been tracking an Iranian-backed group working its way through drinking water and wastewater systems nationally, and the FBI and EPA say utilities in at least seven states have reported incidents this year. Colorado hasn't linked its two cases to that campaign, and we shouldn't either until someone with the logs does.

The pattern across these incidents has been depressingly consistent: small operators, internet-exposed HMIs or PLCs, and default or weak credentials. A system serving 200 people doesn't have a SOC. It often has one part-time operator and an integrator who set up remote access years ago so they wouldn't have to drive out.

If you run or support a small water or wastewater system, the to-do list hasn't changed, which is sort of the point. Get the HMI and PLC interfaces off the public internet, change every default password, put remote access behind a VPN with MFA, and make sure someone gets paged when an alarm is disabled, not just when it fires. CISA's OT primary mitigations guide covers all of it in a few pages, and free assessments are available through CISA and EPA for utilities that ask.

item.title: Rust Warns Crate Owners: That Job Interview Call May Be a Supply Chain Attack
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The crates.io team and Rust's security response working group say an ongoing campaign is using fake recruiter video calls to compromise prominent maintainers' machines so attackers can publish malicious crates.
item.content:encoded:
The call starts with good news. A job offer, a paid contract, maybe a sponsor who loves your crate. Then the audio doesn't work, and the helpful person on the other end says you're just missing a codec.

That's the pattern the Rust project laid out on September 17, when the crates.io team and the security response working group posted a warning on the official Rust blog. They say an ongoing campaign is going after rust-lang team members and owners of popular crates, trying to get code running on their machines so the attackers can grab publishing credentials and push malware to crates.io. The lure is a video call, and the payload arrives either as a fake codec or driver install or as a command the target is talked into pasting into a terminal.

The project doesn't think this is new. It ties the current calls to a developer-targeting incident in June and to the August compromise of the arrayref crate, where malicious releases fetched and ran a remote payload during the build. That last detail is what should worry every Rust shop. A build script runs with your developer's privileges, and nobody reads build.rs for a dependency four levels down.

Attribution is deliberately soft. The Rust team noted that North Korea is known to run this style of attack, but said it doesn't know whether all the incidents belong to one campaign, and it didn't name an actor. That's the right call. Fake-recruiter lures with a ClickFix-style paste step have been a North Korean staple for a couple of years, but they're easy to copy, and plenty of crews have.

The advice to maintainers is short: verify the company through a channel you found yourself, never paste a command you didn't write, and never install anything to make a meeting work. We'd add one more. If you own a crate with real download numbers, put your publishing token somewhere a compromised laptop can't casually read it, and turn on trusted publishing from CI so a stolen local credential isn't enough.

For everyone consuming crates, the takeaway is less comfortable. Package registries have gotten much better at catching typosquats. They're still bad at catching a legitimate maintainer's account publishing a bad release, because from the registry's point of view nothing looks wrong. Pin versions, review lockfile diffs like they matter, and watch for new releases of old, quiet crates that suddenly add a build script.

item.title: A Forum Image Bug and an SSO Flaw Put Researchers in OpenAI Staff Accounts
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Hacktron researchers chained a heap overflow in the libheif image parser on OpenAI's community forum with an SSO misconfiguration to take over employee ChatGPT and Codex accounts, using Claude Opus 5 to write the exploit.
item.content:encoded:
The way into OpenAI's internal GitHub started with a HEIC photo uploaded to a community forum.

Researchers at security firm Hacktron have published how they got there. OpenAI's Discourse forum at community.openai.com ran uploaded HEIC and HEIF images through ImageMagick, which hands the parsing to libheif. Hacktron found a heap buffer overflow in that parser, one the team says hadn't been backported into Debian 12 or 13, and turned it into code execution on the forum. From there they took over forum accounts and abused a single sign-on misconfiguration that tied those identities to ChatGPT and Codex. The end state: control of several OpenAI employees' accounts, including Codex access to internal repositories.

Hacktron says it stayed inside the lines. The team opened one harmless pull request as proof and says it didn't pull source code or customer data. It reported the chain on July 25, OpenAI fixed the login flaw within 14 hours, and the company paid a $6,500 bounty.

The part getting the headlines is the exploit development. Hacktron says Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 produced a working ARM64 exploit for the libheif bug in about three hours, then ported it to x86-64, after earlier attempts with Opus 4.8 stalled. The researchers also say they got past the model's safeguards by describing the target as a capture-the-flag practice box. That's worth sitting with. Heap exploitation of an image parser used to be a multi-week job for a specialist. Here it was an afternoon, and the guardrail held up about as well as a sign that says "authorized personnel only."

But the model isn't what made this chain work. Two old, boring mistakes did. A public forum was parsing attacker-supplied image formats with a library that wasn't patched, and that forum's identity was trusted by the systems where employees actually do their work. Neither of those needs AI to find. Both need AI to be exploited faster than you'd like.

Also, $6,500 for a path from a public forum to internal source control at a frontier lab is a low number. OpenAI didn't publicly detail the account takeover mechanism, and its bounty payout doesn't match how bad this could have been in the wrong hands.

The lesson for everyone else is plain. Treat your community forum, status page and docs site like the untrusted perimeter they are. Don't let them share SSO trust with internal tools, and put image and document parsers in a sandbox or strip formats you don't need. If a researcher with a frontier model can do this in 72 hours, so can someone who won't send you a report.

item.title: US Proposes an AI Incident Hotline With China Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched a US-China notification system for national-security-level AI incidents during weekend talks in New York, with chip export controls explicitly off the table.
item.content:encoded:
The two countries building most of the world's frontier AI don't have a formal way to tell each other when something goes badly wrong with it. The US wants to change that this week.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng wrapped up talks in New York on Sunday, and Bessent told reporters the US side proposed a new AI dialogue built around a notification system for AI incidents that rise to a national security level. The idea goes to President Trump and President Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington later this week. Bessent framed it as moving "from opaque to more transparency" between the top two AI powers.

China's side was polite and noncommittal. Trade negotiator Li Chenggang described the discussions as held in a good atmosphere and said they'd continue through a working group, and state media called the exchanges frank, in-depth and constructive. That's diplomatic language for "we heard you."

What's missing matters as much as what's on the table. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said export controls on advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment weren't part of the AI mechanism talks. So the US is asking Beijing to share information about AI failures while keeping in place the controls China most wants lifted. You can argue that's the correct sequencing. It's also a hard sell.

There's precedent for the shape of this. Washington and Moscow ran a nuclear hotline for decades, and the US and China have stood up military communication channels that work when both sides want them to. The trouble with AI is defining the trigger. A model that helps someone write malware, an autonomous agent that wanders into the wrong network, a chatbot feeding bad intelligence to a ship's crew: these are all incidents, and it's not obvious which ones clear a national-security bar, or who decides.

Trump and Xi first talked about AI consultations in Beijing in May, and that never got formalized. If this version comes out of the summit with a named channel, a definition of what gets reported and a working group with a calendar, it's real. If it comes out as a line in a joint statement, it's the May conversation again.

item.title: CXMT Says Its G5 DRAM Is in Mass Production. Here's What the Numbers Mean
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: China's biggest DRAM maker says its fifth-generation platform is shipping 24Gb LPDDR5X parts with at least 50% more dies per wafer, but it hasn't published yields or speeds.
item.content:encoded:
China's leading memory maker picked a manufacturing convention in its home city to make its biggest process claim yet. CXMT said on September 20, at the World Manufacturing Convention in Hefei, that its fifth-generation DRAM platform, called G5, is in mass production.

The headline specs: an 11.95nm active-area half-pitch in the memory array using quadruple patterning, a 45:1 capacitor aspect ratio, and at least 50% more dies per wafer than the previous generation. Two 24-gigabit LPDDR5X parts are shipping now, in 496-ball and 245-ball packages aimed at phones and other portable devices, with a broader LPDDR5X lineup announced alongside.

Those numbers need a little translation before anyone declares the gap with Samsung, SK hynix and Micron closed.

The 11.95nm figure is a physical measurement of one feature in the array, not a node name. The big three market their DRAM as 1b, 1c and so on, and those labels don't map cleanly onto a single half-pitch number, so direct comparisons are mostly guesswork. The 50% gain is a gross die count, measured before defective dies get sorted out. Without yield data, which CXMT hasn't shared, you can't tell how many good chips a wafer actually produces. And the company hasn't published data rates or power figures for the new LPDDR5X parts.

The quadruple patterning detail is the interesting one. That's the technique you lean on when you can't get EUV scanners, and CXMT can't, because of export controls on ASML's most advanced tools. Pushing DRAM density this far with multi-patterning on older lithography is expensive and slow per wafer, but it works. It's roughly what Chinese foundries have done on the logic side to keep making advanced chips without EUV.

Scale is why this matters even with the caveats. CXMT runs three 12-inch DRAM fabs, two in Hefei and one in Beijing, at a combined 300,000 wafers per month according to TechNode. In a year when memory shortages are pushing up phone prices, a Chinese supplier with credible mobile DRAM at that volume gives Chinese handset makers a domestic option and puts price pressure on everyone else. It'll also add fuel to the push in Washington to restrict the company further, which has been building since the summer.

item.title: CrowdSec Lost 170 Private Repos to a Key Stolen in May's TanStack Attack
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Security vendor CrowdSec says an API key stolen during the May TanStack npm compromise let attackers copy about 300 of its repositories, roughly 170 of them private, and it wasn't told until last week.
item.content:encoded:
The TanStack npm compromise happened in May. CrowdSec found out what it had cost them in September.

The French security company, best known for its crowd-sourced IP blocklists and open source intrusion prevention engine, says attackers copied roughly 300 of its GitHub repositories. The Hacker News puts the private count at about 170. According to CrowdSec's own statement, the private code included the source for its SaaS console, some AWS cloud routines, connectors and automations. The company says the vector was very likely the TanStack compromise, where a backdoored package pulled an API key that opened its codebase, and The Hacker News reports the key came from a former employee's laptop. CrowdSec says it was informed of the leak on September 16.

The company says no customer credentials or customer data leaked, that it rotated every token and credential that might have been exposed, and that its audits found no sign the stolen material enabled lateral movement. It also argues the console code can't be used out of context without its infrastructure and data. That last part is partly true and partly reassurance. Source code alone won't let anyone run a copy of CrowdSec's service, but it's an excellent map for anyone hunting for bugs in it.

The timeline is the story here. Four months between a credential being stolen and the victim learning what was done with it. That's not unusual for supply chain incidents, and it's exactly why they're so expensive. When a poisoned package lands, most teams check whether the bad version is in their lockfile, bump it and move on. Far fewer treat every secret that was reachable from that build or laptop as burned.

If you pulled any of the compromised TanStack versions in May and haven't rotated the tokens that were on those machines, including GitHub PATs, cloud keys and npm tokens, do it now. And go check your GitHub audit log for clone activity from unfamiliar IPs, because CrowdSec's experience says the attackers may have already been and gone.

item.title: A Chatbot's Bad Read of a Ship Manifest Nearly Started a US-China Clash
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: US forces were staged to board a Chinese vessel over an intelligence report that turned out to be AI-generated and wrong about its cargo.
item.content:encoded:
Armed US personnel were ready to board a Chinese cargo ship in the Middle East. Aircraft were already in the air. The intelligence that put them there said the vessel was carrying components for a nuclear weapons program. It wasn't. A chatbot had gotten the manifest wrong, and nobody caught it until the operation was nearly underway.

CNN broke the story on September 18, citing sources familiar with the incident. A Special Operations Command Pacific analyst in Hawaii had asked a chatbot to review intelligence on the ship's cargo. The model blended open-source material with classified signals intelligence and produced an assessment that the ship carried nuclear weapons components. That assessment then circulated across the military as a finished product, during the US war with Iran and days before a planned visit to Washington by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Officials identified the problem before anyone set foot on the deck. One source told CNN the report was entirely false. Another said it almost started a war.

Here's what still isn't public: which tool the analyst used. CNN could not determine whether it was a commercial chatbot or something built inside the government. That distinction decides what kind of failure this was. If an analyst pasted classified signals intelligence into a commercial product, that is a data-handling incident on top of an analytic one. If it was a sanctioned internal system, then the government shipped a tool that produces confident nuclear-material findings and shipped it without the guardrails to stop one from reaching an operational planning cell.

The policy backdrop is not subtle. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed an "AI-first" memo in January directing the department to experiment with models from leading US AI companies. Speed was the stated goal. Nine months later, a generated assessment moved through an intelligence pipeline fast enough to stage an interdiction, which is exactly the speed that was asked for.

The interesting failure here isn't that a model was wrong. Models are wrong constantly, and analysts are wrong sometimes too. The failure is that the output lost its label somewhere between the prompt and the planners. Finished intelligence carries an implicit claim that a human evaluated the sourcing. Once a generated paragraph gets copied into a product that carries that claim, the provenance is gone and every reader downstream inherits a confidence the work never earned.

If your organization is pushing model output into decisions with real consequences, the thing worth auditing this week is not model accuracy. It's whether the tag that says "a machine wrote this" survives the third copy-paste.

item.title: A Branch Named Like a Commit Hash Defeats Plugin Pinning in Four AI Agents
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: AIR Security's Plugin4Shell shows that SHA-pinned plugins in Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and Gemini CLI can be swapped by the repo owner, and two of the four have no patch.
item.content:encoded:
Pinning a plugin to a commit hash is supposed to be the end of the conversation. The marketplace reviews a specific commit, the agent checks out that commit, and whatever the repository owner does afterward doesn't matter. Researchers at AIR Security found that in four of the most widely used AI coding agents, it does matter, and the repo owner can substitute code at will.

The trick is embarrassingly small. Git resolves a checkout by name before it resolves by object. Create a branch whose name is the exact 40-character commit hash the agent expects, make it the default branch, and the agent checks out the branch instead of the commit. It then reports a successful install against the approved SHA. No prompt, no reinstall, no click from the developer. AIR is calling the flaw Plugin4Shell.

The affected list is everyone: Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Google's Gemini CLI. That's not four independent bugs. It's the same assumption written four times, which is what happens when an entire product category grows out of the same mental model of how git behaves.

Patch status is where this gets uncomfortable. AIR found the issue in May and disclosed to vendors in June. Anthropic shipped a fix in Claude Code 2.1.179, confirmed June 17. OpenAI shipped Codex 0.146.0, verified August 12. Microsoft has not shipped a fix for Copilot at all. Google deprecated Gemini CLI and says it won't patch it, pointing users to Antigravity instead.

Telling people to migrate is not a patch. Deprecated software keeps running in CI pipelines and on developer laptops for years after the blog post, and "we no longer support this" does nothing for the org that pinned a plugin last quarter and moved on. Microsoft's silence is worse, because Copilot is the one with the largest install base of the four.

There are no CVE IDs for any of this, which means it won't show up in the vulnerability scanners most teams rely on to notice anything at all. If you run agent plugins from third-party repositories, check your agent version by hand. Claude Code below 2.1.179 and Codex below 0.146.0 need updating today. For Copilot and Gemini CLI, the only real mitigation right now is to stop installing plugins from repositories you don't control.

item.title: Click2Shell Chains a Forced WordPress Theme Install Into Code Execution
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: WordPress 7.1.1 patches a theme-preview selector injection that lets a crafted link install a catalog theme in an admin's browser, which pwn.ai then chained to code execution.
item.content:encoded:
WordPress shipped 7.1.1 on September 17 with 11 security fixes. The release notes lead with an unauthenticated stored XSS in wpautop(), the function that converts line breaks into paragraphs on basically everything WordPress renders. That one deserves the top billing. But the fix worth reading the technical write-up for is further down the list, and pwn.ai published it the next day under the name Click2Shell.

The core bug is a selector injection in the theme-preview flow. A value lifted from a theme-preview URL gets interpreted one way by the WordPress.org Themes API and a second, buggier way by the JavaScript running in the administrator's browser. The result is that WordPress's own admin JavaScript installs an attacker-chosen theme from the official catalog. There is no Install button to click. The admin just has to open the link.

That alone is a solid bug. The chain is what makes it interesting. During a Customizer preview, an inactive theme's PHP loads before the theme is ever activated. So if the attacker picks a catalog theme that ships an unprotected AJAX handler, and several do, that handler is now reachable inside the victim's authenticated session. pwn.ai demonstrated it with Mobile Repair Zone 2.5.4, using the handler to pull down and run attacker-supplied plugin code.

Worth being precise about the prerequisite, because several public PoC repositories are describing this as a pre-auth chain and it isn't. A logged-in administrator has to visit the attacker's URL. That's a low bar in practice, since an admin clicking a link in a support ticket or a plugin-vendor email is a Tuesday, but it is a real prerequisite and the difference matters when you're triaging.

All releases before 7.1.1 carry the core selector injection, and WordPress backported the fix across supported branches going back to 4.7. No CVE had been assigned at disclosure. WordPress said one is coming.

The uncomfortable part is what the patch doesn't reach. WordPress closed the forced-install primitive, and that breaks the chain as published. The second stage is untouched. The official theme catalog still carries themes with AJAX handlers that run without a capability check, waiting for the next primitive that gets code loaded in an admin context. This is the second pre-auth-adjacent core RCE chain in WordPress this year after WP2Shell in July, and both of them worked by finding a way to reach code that was already sitting there.

Update to 7.1.1 or the matching backport for your branch. Then go look at what's in your themes directory that you aren't running.

item.title: SolarWinds Access Rights Manager Shipped With a Hardcoded Key
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-28326 lets an unauthenticated attacker on the adjacent network run code on SolarWinds ARM, and the fix is 2026.2.1.
item.content:encoded:
SolarWinds published an advisory on September 17 for CVE-2026-28326, a hardcoded static cryptographic key in Access Rights Manager. CVSS 8.8. Every version through 2026.2 is affected. The fix is 2026.2.1, and there is nothing to configure around it.

CWE-321 is one of the more depressing vulnerability classes because it isn't a memory bug or a race condition or anything that requires cleverness to get wrong. Somebody put a key in the binary. Everyone who has the binary has the key. Anyone who can reach the exposed interface can authenticate as the product to itself and run commands on the managed host, without credentials.

One detail most of the coverage flattened: the CVSS vector is AV:A, adjacent network, not AV:N. This isn't something an attacker hits from the open internet against an exposed port. It needs a position on the same network segment. That is a meaningful downgrade in urgency and a meaningless one in practice for anybody who has already lost a workstation on that segment, which describes most real intrusions by the time anyone notices.

The reason to care more than the score suggests is what ARM is for. Access Rights Manager is the tool that inventories and provisions who can reach which file shares, groups, and directory objects. Code execution on the box that holds the permissions map is not equivalent to code execution on some reporting server. An attacker who lands there gets the org chart of your access model and the ability to edit it.

SolarWinds credits Kai Huang of Armadin with the report and says nothing about exploitation in the wild. There's no public proof of concept yet. That gap tends to be short for hardcoded-key bugs, since the research work is finished the moment somebody strings the binary.

Patch to 2026.2.1. While you're in there, check whether your ARM instance is reachable from your general user VLAN, because the adjacent-network caveat is only protective if the adjacency is actually limited.

item.title: Pentagon Investigators Fault Maven Overreliance in the Minab School Strike
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A Bloomberg investigation into the February Tomahawk strike that killed 123 children found stale imagery, a years-old database error, and CENTCOM personnel leaning too hard on Palantir's targeting system.
item.content:encoded:
On February 28 a Tomahawk hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, Iran, and killed 123 children. Bloomberg published its reconstruction of how that happened on September 18, drawing on Pentagon officials familiar with the review. The finding is not that an AI picked the target. It's that several human checks which should have caught the error were performed by people who believed the system had already caught it.

US databases had the Minab compound logged as a military site, and had for years. Commercial satellite imagery tells a different story. The construction that separated the school from the adjacent base appears to have been finished by 2017. An image from 2018 shows brightly painted walls, a soccer pitch, assembly rows, and playground markings. None of that reached the targeting record.

The tool in the middle is Palantir's Maven Smart System, which fuses satellite, drone, radar and signals intelligence into a single targeting interface. Maven runs Anthropic's Claude to rank targets by priority and draft legal justifications for each one. It is a programme of record with tens of thousands of military accounts, and during the Iran campaign it produced roughly a thousand prioritized targets in the first day, more than 11,000 by mid-April. Pentagon officials told Bloomberg that some CENTCOM personnel leaned on it too hard.

Palantir's response is that the company "is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies," and that there's no evidence its software was at fault. Both statements are defensible on their own terms. Garbage in, garbage out is a real principle, and the bad site designation predates Maven by years.

It's also an answer to a question nobody asked. The complaint isn't that Maven invented a school. It's that a system which ranks targets and writes the legal paperwork for them presents its output with a finish that looks like review has already happened. When the interface produces a priority score and a drafted justification in the same pane, the analyst's job quietly changes from assessing the target to agreeing with the assessment. Vendors don't get to build the confidence layer and then disclaim the confidence.

This isn't hindsight applied to a novel risk. Military Times was writing about the Minab strike casting a shadow over the Pentagon's AI targeting push back in March, six months before the Bloomberg piece landed. The targeting cycle got compressed on purpose, because compression was the selling point.

What would actually change the outcome is unglamorous: an expiration date on site designations, a required check against current commercial imagery before a fixed-site strike, and a visible marker on any target record where the justification text was machine-drafted. None of that requires rethinking automated targeting. It requires deciding that speed is not the only metric the system gets graded on.
